content.value:
A robot that doesn't know where it is can't plan where to go.

Odometry is the technique of estimating robot position by tracking how far the robot has moved across the ground.

The right way to do it is with dead wheels — unpowered, spring-loaded encoder wheels that ride along the ground. They're not driven by motors, so they don't suffer from wheel slip.

Why not use the drive motor encoders? Because drive wheels slip. When a wheel spins under power, it can lose traction. The encoder says the wheel turned 500 ticks, but the robot only moved 400 ticks' worth of distance. That error accumulates into drift.

A dead wheel is an omni wheel attached to an encoder, mounted on a spring-loaded arm that presses it against the ground.

Because it's not driven by a motor, it only turns when the robot actually moves. No motor torque means no slip.

Two common setups:

Two-pod: one forward pod + one strafe pod + an IMU for heading. This is what Pinpoint uses.

Three-pod: two forward pods (left and right) + one strafe pod. The forward pods' difference gives you heading — no IMU needed.

Both track the robot's full 2D position using unpowered encoder wheels.

steps.title: Quiz: dead wheels vs. drive encoders

content.question: Why are dead wheels better than drive motor encoders for odometry?
options: Dead wheels don't slip because they're not powered — they only turn when the robot actually moves
Dead wheels are required by FTC rules

content.value:
Odometry is relative — it tracks movement from a starting point.

You must give the localizer a starting pose: (startX, startY, startHeading). If that initial value doesn't match where the robot actually sits on the field, every position estimate afterwards will be off by the same amount.

A one-inch error at the start means a one-inch error for the entire match.

Under the hood, the localizer reads ticks from each dead wheel every cycle, converts them to distances, and updates an (x, y, heading) pose.

You don't write that math. Localization libraries (like Pedro Pathing's localizer) handle it:

You configure the dead wheel positions, wheel diameter, and ticks-per-revolution. The library reads the encoders, applies IMU fusion if available, and gives you a clean pose every cycle.

Pinpoint does the same thing — but on its own chip, reporting the finished pose over I2C.

Your job: configure the hardware correctly and trust the pose you get back.

content.question: What does a localization library do for you?
options: Reads dead wheel encoders, runs the math, applies sensor fusion, and returns a clean pose — you just configure it
